text: You've now seen four separate frameworks in this chapter — SOC 2, ISO 27001, PCI DSS, and HIPAA. An organization can easily be subject to three of those at once. If it built a completely separate control implementation for each one, the overhead would be enormous. Mature compliance programs don't do that — they build one real control and map it against every framework's matching requirement.

Take a concrete example: a quarterly review where a manager confirms each person's access to a production system still fits their current role, and removes anything that doesn't. That one control, evidenced once, satisfies SOC 2's logical access criterion, ISO 27001's Annex A access-rights review control referenced in the Statement of Applicability, and PCI DSS's need-to-know access requirement if that system sits inside the Cardholder Data Environment.

The document that makes this explicit is a control mapping, or crosswalk — one row per internal control, with columns showing which specific requirement in each framework it satisfies. Modern GRC tooling automates exactly this: tag one control object against SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS requirement codes, and uploading one piece of evidence updates all three at once. That's also why adding a new framework gets cheaper over time, not harder — most of the real engineering work was already done.

But a crosswalk isn't a universal translator, and a careful compliance engineer knows where it stops working. PCI DSS sometimes needs more specific technical evidence than a general access review captures. A control scoped to all production systems might not line up cleanly with the narrower Cardholder Data Environment. And if cadence requirements differ — monthly versus quarterly — the control has to be built to the strictest one required, never the most lenient.

A real crosswalk documents those gaps honestly instead of papering over them, and that honesty is exactly what separates real compliance engineering from a GRC tool being used to manufacture an illusion of coverage. That closes Chapter 5 on regulatory compliance frameworks. Chapter 6 turns outward, to third-party and vendor risk — because once your own controls are solid, your vendors' weaknesses become the next real gap worth closing.
